title: 2026 Midterm Election: What Parties Are Proposing to Bring Down Inflation
summary: The party that wins a majority could shape how Congress addresses inflation. Here’s a comparison of each side's proposals.
body_markdown:
Inflation has remained above the Federal Reserve’s 2% goal heading into the November 3 midterms. Consumer prices went up 3.7% over the 12 months through September, while core prices increased 2.6%.1 For a household that spends $72,000 a year, a 3.7% increase means paying about $2,664 more to buy the same goods and services ($72,000 × 3.7%). The election could determine which affordability bills advance in Congress, but it will not change prices on its own. Democrats and Republicans are proposing different bills to manage household costs, taxes, trade, energy and regulation. Congress can influence inflation through fiscal and economic policy, while the Federal Reserve sets interest rate policy. Here is a breakdown of what each party is promising, how current legislation compares and the potential impact on your finances.

## What Democrats Are Proposing


Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer began 2026 by making affordability a central theme. He identified healthcare, housing, groceries, childcare, energy expenses and tariffs as pressures on household budgets.2


House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries also made affordability a priority by introducing the “Fighting for an Affordable America” initiative ahead of the midterm elections. The effort included working groups that focused on housing, gas and utilities, groceries and goods, caregiving and healthcare.3


Democratic lawmakers have pursued those priorities through four bills and one policy roadmap targeting[tariffs](https://smartasset.com/taxes/who-pays-tariffs) , prescription drug prices and grocery costs. The four bills are proposed legislation, while the Senate Finance roadmap is a request for information that could help shape future policy.


Each bill would generally need to pass both chambers of Congress and receive presidential approval, or overcome a veto, to become law. The table below summarizes all five measures:


Proposal Lawmakers Introduced Main Provisions Status (October 2026)


Reclaim Trade Powers Act4 Senators Tim Kaine and Raphael Warnock 2026 Would repeal Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 Referred to Senate Finance; repeal would remove that authority without eliminating separate Section 301 duties


End Trump’s Tariff Tax Act5 Senators Chuck Schumer, Ron Wyden, Tim Kaine and others 2026 Would terminate specified import duties, repeal Sections 122 and 338, and authorize refunds for covered payments Introduced in September and referred to Senate Finance


Lowering Drug Costs for American Families Act6 Representatives Frank Pallone Jr., Richard Neal and Bobby Scott 2025 Would expand Medicare drug negotiations and extend certain pricing protections beyond that program Referred to three House committees


Senate Finance drug-pricing roadmap7 Senators Ron Wyden, Catherine Cortez Masto, Peter Welch, Ruben Gallego and others 2026 Requests feedback on negotiation policy, patient expenses and pharmaceutical-market changes Request for information rather than legislation


Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act8 Senators Ben Ray Luján, Jeff Merkley, Jacky Rosen, Kirsten Gillibrand and Martin Heinrich 2026 Would prohibit grossly excessive food charges and specified surveillance-based pricing practices Referred to Senate Commerce


The two[tariff](https://smartasset.com/taxes/tariff-vs-tax) bills address different ways the president can impose taxes on imported goods. On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that a federal emergency law did not give President Trump the authority to impose certain tariffs.9 The administration then used a different law, Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, to add a temporary 10% tax on many imports.10


In March 2026, Senators Tim Kaine and Raphael Warnock introduced the Reclaim Trade Powers Act to repeal Section 122, which the administration had used to impose the surcharge. The temporary 10% import tax expired in July, but the bill would prevent future tariffs based on the same authority. It would not eliminate other duties imposed under Section 301.


The End Trump’s Tariff Tax Act would go further by removing certain[tariffs](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/tariffs-definition-examples) imposed under several laws. It would also require the government to refund some duties already paid by importers.


Proposed changes to prescription drug pricing could affect both[Medicare](https://smartasset.com/data-studies/medicare-payout-preferences-2025) beneficiaries and people with private insurance. Medicare currently negotiates prices for a limited number of medications, while the Lowering Drug Costs for American Families Act would expand the negotiation program and extend certain prescription pricing protections to commercial coverage.


Senate Finance Committee Democrats are examining broader measures to reduce medication expenses, including expanded negotiations and lower out-of-pocket costs for patients. Their roadmap seeks public feedback on potential reforms but is not legislation. The responses could help inform future legislative drafting.


The Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act would prohibit retail food stores from charging grossly excessive prices or using certain personal information to set different prices for individual consumers. The Federal Trade Commission would issue rules and enforce the restrictions, while sellers could defend increases tied to costs outside their control.


## What Republicans Are Proposing


Republican leaders have emphasized lower taxes, increased domestic energy production and reduced federal regulation as ways to address affordability. Senate Majority Leader John Thune pointed to tax cuts as a way to help households cope with higher prices by reducing how much they owe in[federal income taxes](https://smartasset.com/taxes/income-taxes) .


In September, Thune cited the[2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)](https://smartasset.com/taxes/heres-how-the-trump-tax-plan-could-affect-you) as an example, which made lower[individual income tax rates](https://smartasset.com/taxes/current-federal-income-tax-brackets) and a larger standard deduction permanent, expanded the child tax credit and introduced deductions for qualifying tips and overtime pay.


These provisions can leave eligible households with more after-tax income to cover rising expenses, although they do not directly reduce the prices that consumers pay or lower the[inflation rate](https://smartasset.com/retirement/how-to-account-for-inflation-in-retirement-planning) .


Alongside tax and regulatory measures, Republicans have also backed policies intended to expand domestic energy production and reduce electricity and housing costs. Increased energy supply could help limit some price pressures, although the effects depend on market conditions and how quickly new projects develop.


These efforts use different mechanisms, from tax relief and executive action to voluntary commitments and legislation. The table below shows what each measure does, whether it is already in effect and how it could affect household costs:


Measure Lawmakers or Administration Introduced or Enacted Main Provisions Related to Affordability Status (October 2026)


One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans 2025 Permanently lowers individual income tax rates, expands the child tax credit, provides qualifying deductions for tips and overtime income, and makes the larger standard deduction permanent Enacted; provides tax relief to eligible households but does not directly reduce inflation


Executive Order 1415411 President Donald Trump January 2025 Directs agencies to promote domestic energy development, review regulations and remove barriers to permitting In effect; potential effects on energy prices depend on production and market conditions


Ratepayer Protection Pledge12 Trump administration and participating technology companies 2026 Seeks voluntary commitments for data-center developers to cover additional electricity generation and grid costs Voluntary initiative rather than legislation


Ratepayer Protection Act13 Representatives Gabe Evans and Kathy Castor June 2026 Would require regulators and certain utilities to consider making large-load customers, including data centers, responsible for infrastructure costs attributable to their electricity use Passed the House; Senate cloture vote failed September 3014


21st Century ROAD to Housing Act15 Representatives French Hill and bipartisan congressional supporters Introduced 2025; enacted 2026 Addresses housing supply, financing barriers and development rules intended to improve housing affordability Signed into law July 2026; implementation and effects on housing costs will take time


Expanding domestic energy production could help slow increases in fuel and electricity prices by increasing supply. However, new projects take time, and prices depend on demand and other market conditions.


The data-center measures aim to prevent costs associated with serving large electricity users from being shifted to other customers. Housing legislation seeks to increase the number of available homes, which could ease pressure on rents and[home prices](https://smartasset.com/data-studies/home-price-increases-2026) over time. Neither approach guarantees lower costs.


Together with tax relief, these policies could help households manage rising expenses, but their[effects on the overall inflation rate](https://smartasset.com/personal-finance/types-of-inflation) remain uncertain.

## How Current Legislation Compares With Party Proposals


[Republicans and Democrats proposed different ways to address inflation](https://smartasset.com/retirement/inflation-under-trump-vs-biden) , but not all of their plans have become law. Some measures, including the 2025 tax cuts, Medicare’s negotiated drug prices and the bipartisan housing law, are already in effect. Others would require further action by Congress. The table compares existing policies, each party’s proposals and measures supported by both:


Area Current 2026 Policy Democratic Proposals Republican Position or Proposals Bipartisan Measures


Tariffs Existing duties under Sections 232 and 301 remain in effect.16 Repeal specified tariffs and restrict presidential authority Retain tariffs as a trade and industrial policy tool Some Republicans backed Senate resolutions challenging tariffs in 2025, including a measure concerning Canada that the House did not take up.17


Energy Federal actions support domestic production and faster permitting Focus on energy affordability, grid costs and consumer protections Expand domestic production and continue regulatory rollbacks Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House but stalled in the Senate


Housing 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act enacted in July 2026 Additional affordability, tenant and supply proposals Implement the law and reduce construction barriers 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, supported by lawmakers from both parties


Prescription drugs Negotiated prices for the first 10 Medicare Part D drugs took effect January 1, 2026.18 Expand negotiation and extend protections beyond Medicare Emphasize competition, patent and pharmacy-market reforms Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act passed the Senate by unanimous consent.19


Taxes 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act is in effect Targeted relief for healthcare, housing and household costs Preserve or expand the current tax structure Support varies by tax provision


The proposals would affect inflation and[household expenses](https://smartasset.com/taxes/tax-breaks-household-expenses) differently. Lower prescription drug prices could help affected patients without significantly changing overall inflation. More housing supply could slow increases in rents and home prices, but construction takes time. Tax cuts leave eligible households with more money without directly lowering prices.


The Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act, from Senators John Cornyn and Richard Blumenthal, targets patent practices that can delay competition from lower-cost biosimilar drugs. The bill has not yet passed Congress.


## What Needs to Happen Before Proposals Could Affect Inflation


Interest rates, which the Federal Reserve uses to influence inflation and economic activity, fall outside Congress’s direct control. The agency sets them independently, using monetary policy to pursue stable prices and maximum employment. The[Fed aims for 2% inflation](https://smartasset.com/investing/relationship-between-interest-rates-and-inflation) over the longer run, measured by the annual change in the personal consumption expenditures price index.


On October 28, the Fed kept its benchmark interest rate target range at 3.75% to 4%. Two of its 12 voting members wanted to raise rates by 0.25 percentage points. The agency said inflation remains elevated and that more economic data will help it decide the appropriate policy stance to return inflation to its 2% goal.20


Until inflation slows, savings earning interest near the Fed’s current range may barely keep pace with rising prices once taxes are included. A $20,000 balance in a high-yield savings account earning 4% would generate $800 in annual interest ($20,000 × 4%). Interest is taxed as ordinary income, so a saver in the 22% federal bracket would owe $176 ($800 × 22%), leaving $624 after tax.


At the same time, 3.7% inflation would raise the cost of what that $20,000 could buy by $740 ($20,000 × 3.7%). In this example, the saver would fall about $116 short of keeping pace with inflation over the year ($740 − $624), even though the account balance grew. The example assumes a constant interest rate and no state income tax.


The midterm elections could change which party controls congressional committees and votes, but election results alone would not turn proposals into law. A bill generally must pass both chambers in the same form before going to the president. Congress can override a presidential veto with a two-thirds vote in each chamber.21


Most Senate legislation can require 60 votes to invoke cloture and overcome a filibuster before the Senate reaches a final vote on a bill. Budget reconciliation is not subject to the ordinary 60-vote cloture requirement, but its use is restricted by rules governing budget-related provisions.22


President Trump’s current term runs through January 20, 2029. A Democratic Congress would generally need his signature to enact legislation or enough votes to override a veto. Republican control could make it easier to advance White House priorities, but Senate voting rules and disagreements among lawmakers could still prevent passage.


## Bottom Line


The midterms could influence which economic priorities Congress focuses on next, including tariffs, prescription drug costs, taxes, housing and energy. But election results alone would not immediately change inflation or household expenses. Any new policies still need to move through the legislative or regulatory process, and their effects take time to reach consumers. Inflation will also continue to depend on broader economic conditions, including spending, supply, wages and Federal Reserve policy.
